USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current posture — proceed with the already-announced Section 301 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports as leverage, but do not broaden the escalation further, and keep the negotiation channel open to convert China's stated willingness to increase US purchases into a concrete framework. Avoid any new tariff broadening that would deepen China's agricultural retaliation in the run-up to the 2018 midterms, while preserving the credibility that has already extracted concessions.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is moderate (threat_score +0.3), not existential: the US economy is demonstrably strong — industrial production at 103.2, consumer sentiment at 98.2, the 10-year yield near 2.98% and the broad dollar index at 112 rising (country_health), so there is no material GDP drag yet. The escalation is US-initiated and the US holds the leverage, having secured China's May 19 commitment to 'significantly increase' purchases of US goods (event_timeline 2018-05-19) and a ZTE reprieve deal on June 7. What drives the positive threat reading is real and concentrated: China's retaliatory tariffs on soybeans, aircraft and autos strike the farm belt hard — soybeans are the second-largest US export to China with ~61% of US soybean exports going there, and analysts put the hit from a 25% tariff in the billions with permanent market-share loss risk, in politically pivotal midterm districts in Iowa, North Dakota and Kansas (web_search). Add the strain on ally cohesion from the Section 232 steel/aluminum tariffs (EU, Canada, Mexico retaliation) and the risk of an escalation spiral. That is why the action is 'hold' at 0.0 rather than further escalation — broadening now would maximize farm-belt political cost and ally friction while China has already shown willingness to negotiate, and conceding outright would squander hard-won leverage. Staying the course on the announced tariffs while keeping talks open is the disciplined middle path.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the negotiating line and continue talks with Washington (Liu He/Mnuchin-Ross track) rather than escalate or make further unilateral concessions. We should signal a calibrated, proportionate response if the threatened 25% tariffs on $50B of our goods are actually implemented, but keep the door open since the just-completed ZTE settlement shows the US is willing to walk things back under pressure. Do not pre-emptively concede on structural (Made in China 2025 / surplus) issues, and do not escalate pre-emptively.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is real but bounded, not existential. The US has moved against us across the board — the Section 301 finding on IP/tech transfer, a 25% tariff list on ~$50B of our ICT, robotics and machinery exports (timeline 2018-04-03), and firm-level targeting via the ZTE denial order (2018-04-16), then revived the tariff threat on 2018-05-29 after the May 19 truce collapsed. That is genuine high exposure to export-hub employment and tech self-sufficiency, driving threat_score toward +0.4. But several factors keep this below existential: our macro buffer is strong ($3T+ reserves, $422.5B 2017 trade surplus; country_health/China, web search), CNY is stable, and — critically — the US already walked the ZTE ban back in a June 7 deal that saved a company we considered vital, after China conceded ($1B fine, embedded US compliance team, board/exec changes) but also because the US leadership wanted a larger trade and summit agenda (CNBC/NYT 2018-06-07). That demonstrated US willingness to negotiate rather than max-escalate justifies holding at action_score 0.0: we are not cornered enough to need a capitulation, and escalating into a full tariff war would hurt us more than the US given our surplus position and reliance on US tech components (ZTE dependence on US parts). The disciplined play is to keep negotiating, exploit the US farm-belt exposure we already targeted (soybeans/autos, 2018-04-04), and hold threats in reserve rather than fire them now.
